title: Shakuntala's gandharva marriage
hookLine: a king proposes at an empty hermitage, and Shakuntala says yes to a marriage of her own choosing, on one condition
carry: marriage by your own choice has a place in dharma
last: LIFE, SAFETY AND FOOD EACH MAKE A FATHER.

cards: Who is here? That's the first thing King Dushyanta says at the hermitage. He has been hunting, has left his soldiers behind, and walks into the quiet place where the sage Kanva lives and calls out.

Kanva isn't home. A young woman comes out instead, dressed like an ascetic, and welcomes him the way a host should. Then the king proposes marriage, almost at once, and the story waits to see what she'll say.
What she says is not quite yes.

teach.h: SHE WELCOMES HIM AS A HOST
teach.b: First, the welcome. Shakuntala offers the king a seat and water and asks after his health, the duties of a host, and tells him her father has gone to gather fruit.
The king asks who she is, and she tells him her birth: the sage, the apsara, the birds. Then he asks her to marry him. Her first answer is patience.
Wait for my father, she says. He will give me to you. The king answers with dharma.
The old law books, he says, count eight forms of marriage. In some, a father gives his daughter away with rites and gifts.
One, the gandharva, is made by two people's own choice, and it's lawful for a king. She can give herself.
Here's the teaching under the scene: Hindu tradition has long made room for a marriage of the couple's own choosing, right there in its law books, beside the marriages families arrange.
And Shakuntala does the thing the rest of her story hangs on.

teach.h: YES, IF YOU PROMISE ME THIS
teach.b: She agrees, on one condition: promise that the son born of me will be your heir. The king promises. They marry.

He leaves for his city, saying he'll send an escort. Then Kanva comes home. The epic says he knows what happened through his own inner sight, and he isn't angry; he blesses her and calls the marriage a good one.

teach.h: MARRIAGE BY YOUR OWN CHOICE HAS A PLACE IN DHARMA.
teach.b: Today, in plenty of Indian families, love marriage and arranged marriage still get argued over at dinner.
It's an old conversation, and the epic has a word in it: a love match has its place, and Shakuntala made hers with a promise out loud. And from the city, nobody comes.

how: Hindus know this part of Shakuntala's story from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva, where the meeting and the gandharva marriage take place at Kanva's hermitage.

games.q: you're Shakuntala. a king you've just met says a marriage by your own choice is lawful, and asks you to marry him now. what do you say?
o: yes, if you promise my son will be your heir.
games.why: she agrees on one condition, spoken aloud: her son will rule after him. the king promises, and later that promise goes to court.

practice: Bring to mind something you've agreed to lately: a plan, a job, a favor.
Ask gently whether there was something you needed and didn't say, and let one simple sentence form, the way Shakuntala said hers; you don't have to send it anywhere, just hear it in your own voice.
If you pray, you can bring it into prayer.

wordCard.voice: Shakuntala. The young woman who chose her own marriage, the gandharva way, and said yes only on a promise spoken aloud.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the gandharva form of marriage, made by the couple's own choice, which Dushyanta proposes to Shakuntala.

carryVoice: Your line: marriage by your own choice has a place in dharma. Shakuntala's came with a promise, spoken out loud. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Dushyanta at Kanva's hermitage; Shakuntala's welcome; his proposal; his account of the eight forms of marriage and the gandharva; her condition that her son be heir; Kanva's return and blessing; the boyhood of her son)
Manusmriti 3.21 and 3.32 (the eight forms of marriage; the gandharva defined as union by mutual desire)
